newsitem.title: USA: Snapple guerrilla marketing fails; future in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Snapple guerrilla marketing fails; future in doubt.

text.p: After two years of disappointing sales, Snapple fired its ad agency and went to the streets.
But the soft drink's guerrilla marketing campaign -- a $20 million giveaway of samples on streets corners across the country this summer -- has done little to restore the brand's sagging appeal.
Nearly two years after Quaker purchased the line of ready-to-drink tea and fruit drinks for $1.7 billion, Snapple has yet to perform.
Although Quaker never said so, the campaign to give away millions of bottles of free Snapple beverages this summer was an attempt at a turnaround after two years of weak sales.

But recent reports citing supermarket results for the crucial summer sales period have painted a picture far worse than analysts had predicted, leading to renewed speculation about what Quaker should do with Snapple.

"The fact that Snapple had a bad summer is no major surprise," said John McMillin, an analyst for Prudential Securities. "But it's been worse than expectations, especially given the give-away programme," he said.

The decision for the sampling programme was a mid-season change for Quaker, shifting advertising agencies to Foote, Cone & Belding, Chicago from its long-time agency, Kirshenbaum & Bond, and adopting a direct marketing approach.

"We clearly had a mis-start this season with our consumer communications," Quaker Chairman William Smithburg said in a speech to analysts in mid-September. "At first, reluctant to change too much, we soon realised we needed to broaden consumer awareness and take a totally new approach."

Quaker's earlier campaign, "Threedom=Freedom," from Kirshenbaum, pitched Snapple as the leading alternative, the No. 3, after soft-drink giants Coke and Pepsi. But it was criticised as "insider" campaign that confused new consumers.
Although Quaker may not have expected the promotion to turn around sales, such a highly visible and expensive effort raised expectations for some improvement.

Such expectations were dashed earlier this week when it was reported that A.C. Nielsen supermarket sales data had Snapple fruit juice sales down 15 percent for the 12 weeks ended Sept. 14, and tea sales down 14 percent for the same period.

Quaker spokesman Ron Bottrell said reports pronouncing the sampling campaign a failure were "speculative" because they were based on partial information. The company is due to release sales figures with its third-quarter report Oct. 24.
But Snapple's disappointing sales go far beyond its most recent summer selling season, said marketing consultant Jack Trout, managing partner of Trout & Partners, Greenwich, Conn.

Trout sees Snapple's problems as a comedy of errors. As the first of the natural, new age-type drinks, Snapple caught the interest of a younger, hip set. "It went off like a rocket," Trout said. But a fad can quickly turn. "It's the lack of cool that's really hurting them," Trout said.

Then Snapple encountered competition in the iced-tea segment from the Arizona premium brand, and value-priced entries from Coca-Cola and Pepsi, Trout said. "They wiped out a big chunk of the Snapple brand."

In the ready-to-drink tea segment it once dominated, Snapple has fallen to the No. 3 position, behind Pepsi's No. 1 Lipton Brisk and Coca-Cola's No. 2 Cool From Nestea brand, according to Beverage Marketing Corp. figures. The beverage industry consulting company projects overall 1996 sales in the segment to rise 11.4 percent from 1995.

"What drove Snapple's early growth was its uniqueness," said John O'Neil, analyst at Bankers Trust Securities, New York. "Now, there are a number of other me-too beverages and Snapple doesn't have the cachet it once did."

As for the promotional campaign, it may have contributed to Snapple's "uncool" message, Trout said. Giving your product away "is a real signal that the product is not cool," he said. "This is called panic. It says they may really be having trouble if they're handing it out."
